Empirical Research Plan  

================================================================
1. Identification Strategy  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Strategy:  Difference-in-Differences-in-Differences (DDD) in an industry-by-time panel.

• Dimension 1 – Industry exposure to an economic shock (Shock_it).  
• Dimension 2 – Aggregate capital-market liquidity (Liquidity_t).  
• Dimension 3 – Pre- vs. post-wave (Wave_it).

The estimating equation is

 Wave_it = β₁ Shock_it + β₂ Liquidity_t + β₃ Shock_it × Liquidity_t  
     + α_i + γ_t + X_it δ + ε_it                (1)

where  
Wave_it = 1 if industry i is in a statistically-identified wave during month t; 0 otherwise  
α_i   = industry fixed effects (absorbs time-invariant industry propensities)  
γ_t   = month (or quarter) fixed effects (absorbs economy-wide shocks, including Liquidity_t itself)  
X_it  = time-varying controls (industry size, Herfindahl, past wave indicator, etc.).

Because γ_t absorbs the level of Liquidity_t, β₂ is not estimated; the coefficient of interest is β₃.  It captures whether the marginal effect of an economic shock on the probability of a wave is larger when aggregate liquidity is high.  The design is thus a DDD:  
(i) across industries (high vs. low shocks),  
(ii) across macro states (tight vs. loose capital), and  
(iii) across time (before vs. during the wave window).

Why appropriate?  
• We observe all U.S. industries continuously for 20 years.  
• Industry shocks vary cross-sectionally; liquidity varies only over time.  
• Industry and time fixed effects purge the two main first-order endogeneity concerns: permanent industry attributes and economy-wide events.  
• The interaction term survives both fixed effects and is the clean test of joint necessity.

Secondary question (announcement returns): Use event-study CARs and estimate

 CAR_ij = θ Wave_i,t(j) + φ Controls_ij + α_ind + τ_year + υ_ij

where j indexes individual deals.  θ<0 would indicate adverse selection within waves.

================================================================
2. Treatment and Control  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment definition:  Industry-month cells that simultaneously satisfy  
 HighShock_it = 1 (Shock_it in top tercile of its full-sample distribution) AND  
 HighLiquidity_t = 1 (Credit-spread measure below bottom tercile).  
Treated_it = HighShock_it × HighLiquidity_t.

Controls: all remaining industry-month cells, i.e.  
• High shock but tight liquidity,  
• Low shock but loose liquidity,  
• Low shock & tight liquidity.

Treatment timing: monthly (or quarterly) panel, 1981–2000.

================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A1.  Parallel trends – Absent changes in aggregate liquidity, wave incidence for high- and low-shock industries would have evolved in parallel.  
Plausibility: industry FE, pre-trend tests, and the fact that liquidity shocks are macro-wide lend support, but must be checked empirically.

A2.  Aggregate liquidity is exogenous to the residual industry-specific component of M&A activity after time FE.  
Plausibility: individual industries are too small to affect U.S. credit spreads; plausible.

A3.  No other macro variable interacts with Shock_it in the same functional form as Liquidity_t to generate waves.  
Plausibility: could be violated (e.g., tax policy).  We control for obvious candidates (GDP growth, stock-market level).

A4.  Wave classification error is classical (not systematically related to the interaction term).  
Plausibility: the simulation-based test is mechanical and uses only deal counts, so mis-classification should be unrelated to capital-market conditions.

================================================================
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Threat 1:  Endogenous measurement of “economic shock” (managers may accelerate asset sales in expectation of easy credit).  
Mitigation: instrument Shock_it with lagged, predetermined variables such as industry exposure to exogenous tariff changes or technological patents; alternatively use one-year lag of Shock variables.

Threat 2:  Omitted interacting macro variables (e.g., regulatory events) that coincide with liquidity states.  
Mitigation: include month-by-industry-group linear trends; include controls for industry-specific regulatory dummies (banking, utilities).

Threat 3:  Serial correlation and heterogeneous treatment timing causing biased standard errors.  
Mitigation: cluster two-way (industry and calendar month) and implement wild-cluster bootstrap p-values.

================================================================
5. R Code Outline  
----------------------------------------------------------------  

```r
# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 0.  Libraries
# --------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(lfe)         # for high-dim FE
library(lmtest)      # robustness
library(sandwich)
library(ggplot2)

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Load data  (assumes CSVs in working dir)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
sdc   <- fread("sdc_ma_deals.csv")          # deal-level
shock <- fread("compustat_industry_shocks.csv")  # industry-level monthly shocks
liq   <- fread("agg_liquidity.csv")         # credit-spread & real-rate series
waves <- fread("industry_wave_flags.csv")   # Wave_it flag from simulation test

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Variable Construction
# --------------------------------------------------------------
# a) industry-month panel skeleton
panel <- merge(shock, liq, by = "date", allow.cartesian=TRUE)           # add aggregate variables
panel <- merge(panel, waves, by = c("ff48_industry","date"), all.x=TRUE)

# b) high/low indicators
panel[, HighShock := as.integer(scale(ShockMetric) > quantile(scale(ShockMetric), .67))]
panel[, HighLiq   := as.integer(CreditSpread < quantile(CreditSpread, .33))]
panel[, Treated   := HighShock * HighLiq]

# c) replace NA wave flag with 0
panel[is.na(WaveFlag), WaveFlag := 0]

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  Main Specification (DDD)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
spec1 <- felm(WaveFlag ~ HighShock + Treated | ff48_industry + date | 0 | ff48_industry + date,
              data = panel)
summary(spec1)

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  Robustness: Use continuous measures & logit
# --------------------------------------------------------------
panel[, Shock_std := scale(ShockMetric)]
panel[, Spread_std := scale(CreditSpread)]
panel[, Interaction := Shock_std * Spread_std]

spec2 <- felm(WaveFlag ~ Shock_std + Interaction | ff48_industry + date | 0 | ff48_industry + date,
              data = panel)
summary(spec2)

# Logit with industry & year FE
panel[, year := year(date)]
logit1 <- glm(WaveFlag ~ Shock_std*Spread_std + factor(ff48_industry) + factor(year),
              data = panel, family = binomial(link="logit"))
coeftest(logit1, vcov = sandwich)

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Event-study CARs (announcement returns)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
# build ±3-day CARs for each deal (already pre-calculated and stored)
car <- fread("deal_level_CAR.csv")  # columns: deal_id, CAR, ff48_industry, date, controls…

car <- merge(car, waves[,.(ff48_industry, date, WaveFlag)], 
             by = c("ff48_industry","date"), all.x=TRUE)
car[is.na(WaveFlag), WaveFlag := 0]

car_spec <- felm(CAR ~ WaveFlag + Controls | ff48_industry + year(date) | 0 | ff48_industry,
                 data = car)
summary(car_spec)
```

================================================================
6. Expected Results  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
• β₃ > 0: The marginal effect of an economic shock on the probability of a merger wave is significantly larger (economically and statistically) when capital-market liquidity is abundant.  
Magnitude: A move from tight to loose liquidity (75th → 25th percentile credit spread) is expected to raise the shock-wave elasticity by roughly 10–15 percentage points, increasing the probability of a wave from a base 6 % to about 16 % for high-shock industries.

• Announcement Returns: θ ( WaveFlag ) < 0.  We expect CARs to be 1–1.5 pp lower for in-wave deals, consistent with mild overpayment/adverse selection.

================================================================
7. Validity Checklist (self-assessment, 1 = strong, 0 = weak)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
1. Parallel-trend evidence from pre-treatment leads ………… 0.8  
2. Exogeneity of aggregate liquidity to individual industries …… 0.9  
3. No simultaneous policy shocks correlated with interaction …… 0.6  
4. Correct functional form / no violation of SUTVA ……………… 0.8  
5. Accurate treatment measurement (wave flag & shocks) ………… 0.7  

Overall: 3.8 / 5 – credible but not bullet-proof; robustness and pre-trend tests are essential.
